chief_complaint: empty scrotum on exam of 6-month-old infant
hpi_details: A 6-month-old boy is brought by his parent after an empty left hemiscrotum was noted since birth. He is feeding and growing normally, without groin pain, swelling, fever, vomiting, or urinary symptoms.
ideas: parent wonders whether this is an undescended testis
concerns: The parent is worried that his baby will need surgery under general anesthesia while he is still so small.
expectations: The parent hopes to get an ultrasound scan today to see where the missing testicle is located.
pmh: Born at term; no prior surgery or significant illness

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Undescended Testis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt referral to pediatric urology, with orchiopexy generally performed between 6 and 18 months of age, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: empty scrotum on exam of 6-month-old infant
Key HPI features: An empty left hemiscrotum has been noted since birth without pain, swelling, fever, vomiting, or urinary symptoms.
Objective/Exam findings: Examine the scrotum and inguinal canals for a palpable testis and document laterality; routine imaging is not needed before specialist referral.
Relevant background/PMH: Born at term; no prior surgery or significant illness
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Undescended Testis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Using ultrasound to locate a nonpalpable testis before referral; it rarely changes initial management.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring acute painful groin or scrotal swelling, which requires urgent assessment for torsion.
management_principles: Refer promptly to pediatric urology for examination and planned orchiopexy between 6 and 18 months of age
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Urology evaluation of a 6-month-old boy with an empty left hemiscrotum noted since birth.
red_flags: Acute painful groin or scrotal swelling
Vomiting or inconsolability with possible testicular torsion

must_ask.objective: Timing and prior documentation of the empty scrotum
must_ask.say: When was the empty scrotum first noticed, and was either testis documented in the scrotum after birth?

must_ask.objective: Intermittent descent suggesting a retractile testis
must_ask.say: Have you ever seen or felt the testis in the scrotum, such as when he is warm or relaxed?

must_ask.objective: Screen for acute painful groin or scrotal swelling
must_ask.say: Has he had sudden crying, groin or scrotal swelling, vomiting, or pain when the area is touched?
Was he born early, and is there a family history of undescended testes or genital differences?
Has anyone mentioned a hernia, differences in the penis or urinary opening, or problems passing urine?

history.answer: We brought our 6-month-old son because we cannot feel a testicle on the left side of his scrotum.
We noticed his left side seemed empty right after he was born, and it has stayed that way ever since.
It is only the left side that feels empty; his right testicle has always been down in the scrotum.
He does not seem to be in any pain at all, and he only cries when he is hungry or sleepy.
He has not shown any discomfort or tenderness when we touch his lower belly or groin area.
No, he has never had sudden crying spells or episodes of severe belly or groin pain.
He has not vomited at all, and he keeps his milk down without any trouble.
There is no swelling on either side, and the left side stays empty whether he is lying down or being held.
Even during a warm bath or when he is completely relaxed, the left testicle never drops into the sac.
He moves his legs freely and does not seem bothered or weighed down in his diaper area.
We haven't felt any hard lump or swelling in his scrotum or around his groin.
No, he has not had any fever, chills, or warm skin.
He wets six to eight diapers a day, does not cry while urinating, and has no unusual discharge.
His penis looks normal, the urine comes straight out from the tip, and he has a good strong stream.
The skin on his scrotum looks completely normal, without any redness, dark discoloration, blisters, or odor.
He hasn't had any falls, bumps, or injuries to his groin.
No swelling near his ears or jaw, and no one around him has had mumps.
The pediatrician noted the empty left side at his newborn checkup and recommended rechecking it around six months.
No weight loss, cough, or breathing problems; he has been steadily gaining weight and thriving.
He has never had any urinary catheters, medical procedures, or surgery.
I was reading about it and wondered if this might be an undescended testicle.
I'm terrified that he might have to undergo surgery and be put to sleep when he's only six months old.
I'm hoping you can order an ultrasound today to find out exactly where his testicle is hiding.
He has been very healthy and has had no medical illnesses or hospital stays.
He has never had any surgeries or operations.
He is not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamin supplements.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
He was born at 39 weeks by an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, weighing 3.2 kilograms.
He is rolling over, smiles, tracks objects, and is reaching all of his milestones right on schedule.
His vaccines are completely up to date, including his recent 6-month shots.
There is no family history of undescended testicles, childhood hernias, or fertility issues.
He lives at home with my husband and me in an apartment; both of us are non-smokers and don't drink around him.
He is cared for at home by me and does not go to daycare or have exposure to sick individuals.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 86/52 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 100% on room air.
Well-nourished, well-developed 6-month-old infant resting comfortably in parent's arms in no acute distress.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender, with no palpable abdominal mass or hepatosplenomegaly.
The right testis is fully descended, normal in size, and non-tender in the scrotum; the left hemiscrotum is hypoplastic and empty, and no testis can be milked down into the scrotal sac.
A small, smooth, mobile, non-tender 1 cm ovoid testis-like mass is palpable in the superficial left inguinal canal; no inguinal hernia or lymphadenopathy bilaterally.
Stroking the inner thigh elicits a normal right cremasteric reflex with brisk testicular elevation; the left hemiscrotum remains empty.
Growth parameters are at the 50th percentile for age with normal gross motor tone and age-appropriate developmental milestones.
